title: Analytical and numerical solutions to the non-diffusive Stefan problem
authors: Matthew Van Ham, Minghan Xu, Samuel Huberman
abstract: In this work, the Maxwell--Cattaneo--Vernotte (MCV) equation is used to model the one-dimensional hyperbolic Stefan problem in the limit of a small Stefan number (Ste $\ll$ 1). The solutions are approximated with perturbation series expansions using a reformulation in which time is expressed as a function of the solid-liquid interface position. The first proposed solution is derived in a framework that considers diffusive heat transfer at the phase change interface, for analytic tractability. Two rectification strategies are proposed to address the asymptotic divergence present in this formulation: a rescaled inner solution which is then combined with the outer solution to yield a composite solution, and size-dependent thermo-physical system parameters for better capture of hyperbolic effects at the phase change interface. The resulting interface profiles exhibit a characteristic parabolic-like shape, consistent with diffusive Stefan problem findings, with pronounced early-time hyperbolic effects at larger thermal relaxation times. Parametric studies are done over three pertinent variables in the dimensionless system: the Stefan number ($\mathrm{Ste}$), the dimensionless thermal relaxation time ($\widetilde τ$), and the thermal diffusivity ($α$). The studies suggest that model error scales with the Stefan number in accordance with the theoretical truncation error of the perturbation expansion. Additionally, larger values of $\widetilde τ$ amplify early-time hyperbolic effects, thereby increasing model error, while larger $α$ extends the relative temporal domain over which these hyperbolic effects remain significant, also corresponding to an increase in model error.
summary: This paper tackles the complex Stefan problem using advanced heat transfer models (MCV equation) that account for hyperbolic, non-diffusive effects. It employs perturbation theory and matched asymptotic expansions to derive accurate solutions by combining inner and outer approximations. The results clarify how early-time transient behavior is governed by these hyperbolic terms, which increases model error under certain parameter regimes.
main_problem: The work aims to develop analytical and numerical solutions for the non-diffusive Stefan problem, which models phase change dynamics under non-Fourier heat transfer conditions.
main_result: The study successfully derives composite solutions by combining inner and outer approximations, showing that hyperbolic effects are pronounced at early times and increase model error when thermal relaxation time or diffusivity is large.
method: Perturbation series expansions are used for small Stefan numbers, combined with a matched asymptotic construction involving rescaling time to capture initial transient dynamics.
model_or_system: The physical system is a one-dimensional domain undergoing phase change (freezing/melting) governed by the Maxwell--Cattaneo--Vernotte (MCV) equation, which incorporates hyperbolic heat conduction effects.
key_observables: Interface profiles ($	ilde{x}_i$ vs $	ilde{t}$), temperature profiles ($	heta$), and model error scaling.
important_parameters: Stefan number (Ste), dimensionless thermal relaxation time ($\epsilon	au$), and thermal diffusivity ($\alpha$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes a small Stefan number ($	ext{Ste} \ll 1$) and initially considers diffusive heat transfer at the interface for tractability, though it extends to non-diffusive models.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares hyperbolic and parabolic solutions to the classical 1D Stefan problem. Other figures compare dimensionless interface positions and temperature profiles across varying Ste and $\alpha$ values under different interfacial condition assumptions.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the governing equations (MCV, Stefan condition), applies perturbation theory for small Ste, develops inner/outer solutions to handle asymptotic divergence, proposes composite solutions, and validates results numerically against known limits.
why_interesting: While focused on classical thermodynamics, the mathematical techniques—such as developing matched asymptotic expansions for hyperbolic PDEs with singular initial conditions—are highly relevant to modeling non-equilibrium dynamics in quantum systems or open quantum systems where relaxation times are critical.
